problem: SLAM-based navigation for indoor construction sites is costly and brittle (dynamic, cluttered, texture-poor scenes), and existing VLM/VLN methods lack global planning, long-term memory and multi-floor (stair) handling. Complete construction-scene simulation data for validation is also missing.
motivation: Construction inspection is hazardous and labor-intensive, and quadruped robots could automate it, but they need robust navigation without pre-built high-precision maps. Pre-trained VLMs offer semantic reasoning that could replace geometric feature matching, and BIM provides prior structural knowledge.
key_idea: A two-stage VLM framework: BIM-derived floor plan and scene graph with A* plus VLM path selection produce sub-tasks, then a VLM agent with video and text memory executes discrete actions for a quadruped robot.
insight: Combining BIM-based topological global planning with local VLM control lets a small VLM handle long-horizon, multi-floor tasks without SLAM or maps. The evidence is only qualitative: two demonstrations (room-to-room, stair climbing) plus text-similarity metrics for path descriptions, with no ablations or baselines, so the contribution of individual components (memory, prompts) is not isolated.
method: Navigation data preparation: parse BIM into 2D multi-floor floor plans with Type-Floor-ID coding (S,H,R,D,W,C), and build a heterogeneous scene graph with spatial nodes (rooms, hallways, stairs), component nodes (columns, windows), accessibility edges and inclusion edges (manually extracted).
Path candidate generation: map the natural-language task to start/target nodes and run A* on the scene graph to get N candidate paths.

VLM path selection and description: the VLM takes the floor plan image plus candidate node sequences, picks the optimal path considering complexity, landmark saliency and accessibility, and outputs a first-person global description and a sub-task sequence S.

VLM navigation agent: at each step the input is the last m=20 RGB frames with directional visual prompts, textual memory (capacity ω=10) and the current sub-task with selected scene-specific instructions; the output is JSON with an action sequence (max 2 actions), a done flag and an action rationale.

Structured prompt: task overview, action-space definition {move_forward 0.3 m, turn_left/right 15°, stop}, history memory, navigation strategies (e.g., align with the door or stair center before crossing) and output format.

Simulation environment: a three-story educational building BIM converted to GLB via a Revit plugin and loaded into Habitat 3.0, with a quadruped model (collision radius 0.28 m, height 0.55 m, front camera at 1.0 m, 90° FOV, 1280×720).

setting.observation: egocentric front RGB video (last 20 frames, 1280×720) with direction prompts; BIM floor plan and scene graph as prior
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: move_forward 0.3 m, turn_left/right 15°, stop
setting.privileged: BIM-derived floor plan and manually extracted scene graph used as prior; start/target nodes parsed from the task

numbers.eval_set_note: 20 generated navigation task descriptions compared with human ground-truth descriptions
numbers.extra: uses BIM floor plan and scene graph; text-similarity metrics, not navigation success
numbers.evidence: Table 2 (labelled Table 1): Quantitative evaluation of navigation path description generation; BLEU 64.24, ROUGE-L F1 0.795, Token F1 0.803

numbers_note: No SR/SPL or standard benchmark results; navigation execution is shown only qualitatively (Fig. 6). Only text-similarity metrics for path description are given.
results: Stage-1 path description reaches BLEU 64.24, ROUGE-L F1 0.795 and Token F1 0.803 against human references on 20 tasks. The agent qualitatively completes texture-less room-to-room traversal and stair climbing in the simulated building. No baselines or success-rate metrics are reported.
limitations: Simulation-only validation on a single building with no real robot, so a sim-to-real gap remains; there are no dynamic obstacles and no quantitative navigation metrics or baselines
Relies on cloud VLM latency, VLM hallucination and instability, and manually extracted scene graphs
Evaluation is small (20 descriptions, two qualitative scenarios) and there is no large-scale benchmark
